gregor_intact.label: Ask Gregor at the stable about the day Hartmann left
gregor_intact.log: You asked Gregor at the stable about the day Hartmann left.
gregor_intact.text:
You ask about the day Hartmann left.

He hangs the rein in his hand back on its hook and does not answer at once. Somewhere in the stable a horse shifts its weight and a shoe knocks against stone.

“There was no horse missing from this stable that morning,” he says. “Not one.”

He looks at you once, as though checking whether you have understood what that means. You have not. He does not explain.

gregor_returned.label: Find Gregor at the stable
gregor_returned.log: You spent another while at the stable, and Gregor corrected what he had said before.
gregor_returned.text:
“What I said last time was not right.” He is combing out a chestnut’s mane, and the rhythm of the comb does not break.

“On the third day one of them came back on its own. Stood at the top of the avenue, waiting.”

You ask how it ran back.

“It did not run back,” he says. “The rein had been untied, not broken loose from. Breaking loose leaves a mark, and frays the end. That rein was sound.”

He sets the comb down. “He turned it loose to come home. He did not want it following him.”

gregor_condition.label: Find Gregor at the stable
gregor_condition.log: Gregor gave you the thing he had been keeping.
gregor_condition.text:
He takes you to the last stall at the back of the stable.

“When it came back, the shoe on the off fore was worn more than the near one. That means it had been on a slope, putting its weight down on the right the whole way.”

“The mud on its legs came up to here.” He marks a line on his own calf. “Not road dirt. Bottom-land mud. Black, and it has a smell to it.”

“Something was tangled in the mane. I kept it.” He takes a cloth bundle down off a beam and opens it. Inside is a small handful of dried plant matter.

He hands you the bundle and goes back to his work. He does not say what any of it means. He does not draw conclusions. He hands you what he saw, entire, and the drawing of conclusions is your business.

marta_summer.label: Ask Martha in the kitchen about Hartmann
marta_summer.log: You asked about Hartmann in the kitchen.
marta_summer.text:
There is nobody left in the kitchen but her. The board has been wiped down and she is setting out tomorrow’s things one at a time.

You ask about Hartmann.

“Him.” She puts down an earthenware jar. “He had not been right since the summer.”

“Not right how?”

“Things piling up and not getting done,” she says. “The cow shed on the west holding was reported in June. Old Wendt’s roof was reported last year. I told him three times.”

She wipes her hands on her apron.

“He was not a man who let things go. You want to know that. Before, when the tenants brought something in, he had an answer the same day: if it could be done, when; if it could not, why not. He never fobbed anybody off.”

“And after?”

“After, I would talk to him and he listened.” She thinks about it. “He really was listening. His eyes were on me. But when I had finished he would only nod, and nothing came after it.”

She sets the last jar in its place.

“It was not impatience and it was not dodging me,” she says. “It was as though what I said got as far as him and ran into something else that was already there.”

marta_lastwords.label: Sit in the kitchen in the evening
marta_lastwords.log: Martha told you about the night before Hartmann left.
marta_lastwords.text:
She is not busy tonight. She is sitting on the stool by the board with both hands on her knees.

“That thing you asked me,” she says. “I have been turning it over these last days.”

She looks over towards the range.

“A few days before he went he came into the kitchen. At night, very late; I was clearing up. He stood in the doorway and did not come in.”

“He asked me one thing.”

She stops a moment.

“He asked me whether, if I could have chosen at the start, I would still be doing this.”

“What did you say?”

“I said, ‘What else would I do.’” She says: “My hands were full at the time. I answered without thinking about it.”

She moves her hands to a different place.

“He said, ‘True enough.’ And then he went.”

The kitchen is quiet a while. A coal falls in on itself in the range.

“I have been here forty years,” she says. “Forty years of listening to people. Which couple has been fighting, whose son means to leave, who wants to say a thing and dare not. I know it the moment I hear it.”

“That one time.”

She does not finish the sentence.

elena_papers.label: Ask Elena what Hartmann was like at the end
elena_papers.log: Elena told you about the papers in Hartmann’s room.
elena_papers.text:
She is putting the empty room at the end of the corridor in order, the one next to yours.

You ask her what Hartmann was like in his last weeks.

She sets down the cloth in her hand and stands still.

“Sir, I only clean.”

“I know.”

She looks at the floor a moment.

“The lamp,” she says at last. “The lamp in his room, those last two months, it burned very late every night. Sometimes when I went in in the morning the oil had run dry.”

“And the desk?”

“Papers,” she says. “Different papers every day. What was spread out one day would be put away the next, and a new lot out instead.”

She pauses.

“There was one I saw three times.”

“The same sheet?”

“The same sheet,” she says. “It had been crumpled up, and opened out again, and pressed flat. The creases stayed in it. The first time it was on the desk. The second time it was in the wastepaper basket. The third time it was back on the desk.”

She picks up the cloth again.

“I did not read what was written on it.”

She is looking at you when she says it.

elena_burned.label: Stay late in the office
elena_burned.log: Elena came to the office to find you, and told you something she had been holding back.
elena_burned.text:
She came to find you. It is the first time.

She is standing in the office doorway with nothing in her hands. There is always something in her hands — a cloth, sheets, a bucket. Today there is nothing.

“Sir,” she says. “There is something I have not said.”

She does not wait for you to answer.

“The night before he left, I saw him in the forge-chapel.”

“It was very late. Two o’clock, or later. He was crouched at the edge of the hearth, putting things into it.”

“Putting in what?”

“Paper,” she says. “One sheet at a time. Not a handful thrown in. One at a time. Every sheet he put in, he waited for it to finish burning before he put in the next.”

Her voice is very quiet, and it does not shake.

“There was one he held for a long time.”

She stops.

“He did not burn that one?”

“He burned it,” she says. “But he held it a long time.”

The room goes quiet.

You do not ask her why she was at the forge-chapel at that hour.

She waits a moment, as though waiting for that question.

You do not ask it.

“I should get on,” she says, and goes.

lorenz_question.log: Lorenz told you the question Hartmann once put to him.
lorenz_question.text:
The fire in the hearth is burning low today. He puts a piece in and waits for it to come up on its own.

“You have been here a good many times,” he says. “More than most.”

He sits back down on his own stool.

“So was Hartmann.”

He is not looking at you when he says it, and there is no pause before it. He is carrying on from his own last sentence, not handing you anything.

“He came here more often in his last half year than in the seven before it put together.”

“Did he say anything to you?”

“He asked one question.”

He moves the coals about with the tongs.

“He asked whether, if the work a man does is itself wrong, doing that work better means being further in the wrong.”

“He asked it very politely. As though it were something with nothing to do with him. A technical question.”

He puts the tongs down.

“But a technical question asked that far is not a technical question any more.”

“What did you tell him?”

“I said I did not know.” He says: “I still do not know.”

The fire has come up again. He watches it.

“I should have asked him then why he was asking. I did not ask.”

lorenz_why.log: Lorenz said why he had told you about Hartmann.
lorenz_why.text:
He is already there when you come to the forge-chapel. The fire is exactly right and needs nothing put on it.

He does not speak at once. You sit a while.

“I told you about Hartmann,” he says.

“You did.”

“I should not have.”

He puts his hands on his knees.

“In the position I hold, most of what I know I never went looking for. People walk up to me and say it. When they say it they have not considered that I might pass it on. It does not so much as occur to them, because if it occurred to them they would not say it.”

“People here come to me when something is wrong. Forty years of it,” he says. “If I repeated what I was told, by the fifth year nobody would come.”

A coal splits in the fire.

“So the first thing this trade taught me was how to hold a thing in.”

He is silent a long time.

“And I told you.”

You wait.

“Because he is not here,” he says. “Because it has stopped being a thing that belongs only to him. Everyone on this estate is waiting on an account of it. The tenants are waiting. Martha is waiting. That girl is waiting too.”

“And you are the only one still looking.”

He watches the fire.

“I worked at it a long time before I decided to speak.” He says: “What I was working out was whether saying it would make things better or worse.”

“I could not get it to come out.”

He turns his head to look at you.

“So in the end I guessed. I guessed you were the kind who does something about a thing once he has heard it.”

He looks back at the hearth.

“A man in my trade should not have to guess.”

lorenz_already_told.log: Lorenz said he had already told you that.
lorenz_already_told.text:
You bring up Hartmann.

“I have told you about that,” he says.

He puts a piece of wood in the hearth and waits for it to come up on its own.

“The same words said twice. The second time it is not the same sentence.”
